option_d: Permeable cuticular linings that permit direct nutrient absorption
explanation: Arteries withstand high systolic blood pressure; they feature thick tunica media with smooth muscle and elastic fibers, narrow lumens, and lack valves.
subject: Biology

question: Semilunar valves are located at the base of the:
option_a: Superior and inferior vena cavae
option_b: Subclavian and jugular veins
option_c: Aorta and pulmonary artery
option_d: Coronary arteries and cardiac veins
explanation: Aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves prevent backflow of ejected blood from the great arteries back into the ventricles during ventricular diastole.
subject: Biology

question: Which component of human blood plays the primary role in blood clotting (hemostasis)?
option_a: Erythrocytes (red blood cells)
option_b: Neutrophil granulocytes
option_c: Blood plasma albumin
option_d: Platelets (thrombocytes)
explanation: Platelets adhere to damaged vascular endothelium and release thromboplastin, initiating the enzymatic cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
subject: Biology

question: In the blood clotting mechanism, thrombin catalyzes the conversion of:
option_a: Soluble fibrinogen into an insoluble mesh of fibrin threads
option_b: Insoluble prothrombin into active thromboplastin
option_c: Heparin into anticoagulant antithrombin III
option_d: Hemoglobin into methemoglobin crystals
explanation: Thrombin is an active serine protease that cleaves soluble plasma fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin monomers that polymerize to form the blood clot mesh.
subject: Biology

question: A person with blood group AB is referred to as a universal recipient because their plasma contains:
option_a: Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
option_b: Neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies
option_c: Only anti-Rh D agglutinins
option_d: No ABO red blood cell surface antigens
explanation: Blood group AB erythrocytes express both A and B surface antigens, meaning their plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies; thus, they can receive red cells from A, B, AB, or O.
subject: Biology

question: A person with blood group O is known as a universal donor because their red blood cells:
option_a: Contain both anti-A and anti-B surface antigens
option_b: Possess no cell membranes or cytoplasm
option_c: Lack both A and B antigens on their surface
option_d: Have high concentrations of Rh agglutinogens
explanation: Group O red blood cells lack both A and B agglutinogens; when transfused, recipient antibodies do not attack them, making O blood widely compatible.
subject: Biology

question: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) can occur when a:
option_a: Rhesus-positive mother carries a Rhesus-negative fetus
option_b: Mother with blood group AB gives birth to an infant with blood group O
option_c: Father with blood group O conceives with an Rh-positive mother
option_d: Rhesus-negative mother carries a Rhesus-positive fetus for a second time
explanation: An Rh-negative mother sensitized by Rh-positive fetal blood during a first birth produces anti-Rh IgG antibodies that cross the placenta in subsequent Rh+ pregnancies, lysing fetal red cells.
subject: Biology

question: The liquid portion of blood remaining after all cells and clotting factors (such as fibrinogen) have been removed is:
option_a: Serum
option_b: Plasma
option_c: Lymph
option_d: Chyle
explanation: Serum is blood plasma minus the clotting proteins (fibrinogen and prothrombin); it contains electrolytes, hormones, antibodies, and dissolved nutrients.
subject: Biology

question: The lymphatic system assists the cardiovascular system primarily by:
option_a: Synthesizing hemoglobin for red blood cells in lymph nodes
option_b: Returning excess filtered tissue fluid to the venous bloodstream
option_c: Pumping oxygenated blood directly into systemic arterioles
option_d: Filtering carbon dioxide gas out of cerebral cerebrospinal fluid
explanation: Excess interstitial fluid filtered from capillaries enters lymphatics as lymph, passes through filtering lymph nodes, and returns to the bloodstream via the subclavian veins.
subject: Biology

question: Phagocytosis is carried out in the mammalian bloodstream primarily by:
option_a: Erythrocytes and thrombocytes
option_b: B-lymphocytes and plasma cells
option_c: Neutrophils and monocytes (macrophages)
option_d: Basophils and mast cells
explanation: Neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages are professional phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogenic bacteria and cellular debris.
subject: Biology

question: Antibodies that confer humoral immunity against pathogens are produced and secreted by:
option_a: Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
option_b: Red blood erythrocytes
option_c: Blood platelets
option_d: B-lymphocytes (plasma cells)
explanation: Activated B-lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antigen-specific immunoglobulins (antibodies) to neutralize pathogens.
subject: Biology

question: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is clinically diagnosed when an adult's resting blood pressure consistently exceeds:
option_a: 140/90 mmHg
option_b: 120/80 mmHg
option_c: 100/60 mmHg
option_d: 80/40 mmHg
explanation: Clinical hypertension is generally diagnosed when systolic blood pressure is ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic pressure is ≥90 mmHg on repeated medical measurements.
subject: Biology

question: The central nervous system (CNS) in vertebrates consists of the:
option_a: Cranial nerves and spinal nerves
option_b: Brain and spinal cord
option_c: Sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia
option_d: Sensory receptors and motor effector organs
explanation: The vertebrate CNS consists of the brain enclosed in the cranium and the spinal cord protected within the vertebral column.
subject: Biology

question: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
option_a: Nephron
option_b: Glial astrocyte
option_c: Neuron (nerve cell)
option_d: Myofibril
explanation: A neuron is an excitable cell specialized for receiving, integrating, and conducting electrochemical signals (action potentials).
subject: Biology

question: Which part of a multipolar neuron carries electrical impulses away from the cell body (soma)?
option_a: Dendrite
option_b: Nissl body
option_c: Myelin sheath
option_d: Axon
explanation: Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body, whereas the axon conducts action potentials away from the soma toward target synaptic junctions.
subject: Biology

question: The insulating layer that wraps around many vertebrate axons and accelerates the transmission of nerve impulses is the:
option_a: Myelin sheath
option_b: Neurilemma membrane
option_c: Endoneurium sheath
option_d: Synaptic vesicle layer
explanation: The myelin sheath (produced by Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS) provides electrical insulation, allowing rapid saltatory conduction.
subject: Biology

question: The microscopic gap or junction between the terminal end of an axon and the dendrite of the next neuron is called a:
option_a: Node of Ranvier
option_b: Synapse
option_c: Neuromuscular cleft
option_d: Chiasma
explanation: A synapse is the functional junction across which nerve impulses are transmitted via chemical neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine).
subject: Biology

question: Saltatory conduction of nerve impulses occurs in myelinated axons because the action potential:
option_a: Passes straight through the non-conductive myelin layers
option_b: Diffuses slowly across intracellular neurofilaments
option_c: Jumps from one Node of Ranvier to the next node
option_d: Travels backward along dendritic arborizations
explanation: Myelin prevents ion leakage; voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated at Nodes of Ranvier, allowing the impulse to leap rapidly from node to node.
subject: Biology

question: Which chemical substance acts as a neurotransmitter at mammalian neuromuscular junctions?
option_a: Insulin
option_b: Hemoglobin
option_c: Pepsinogen
option_d: Acetylcholine
explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the primary neurotransmitter released at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions, initiating muscle depolarisation.
subject: Biology

question: A reflex arc represents the neural pathway that coordinates an involuntary response. Its correct sequence is:
option_a: Receptor → Sensory neuron → Interneuron (relay neuron) → Motor neuron → Effector
option_b: Effector → Motor neuron → Relay neuron → Sensory neuron → Receptor
option_c: Receptor → Motor neuron → Brain → Sensory neuron → Effector
option_d: Interneuron → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Effector → Motor neuron
explanation: A classic spinal reflex arc involves: Receptor (detects stimulus) → Sensory neuron → Relay neuron in spinal cord → Motor neuron → Effector muscle/gland.
subject: Biology

question: Which of the following is an example of an unconditioned (inborn) reflex action?
option_a: Riding a bicycle along a busy highway
option_b: Knee-jerk reflex (patellar reflex) upon tapping the patellar tendon
option_c: Typing an essay on a computer keyboard
option_d: Playing a musical piece on a violin
explanation: Inborn (unconditioned) reflexes (e.g. knee-jerk, pupil constriction, withdrawing hand from fire) are automatic, stereotyped, and require no prior learning.
subject: Biology

question: Conditioned reflexes differ from simple inborn reflexes because conditioned reflexes:
option_a: Are coordinated exclusively by the lumbar spinal cord without brain involvement
option_b: Are present at birth and passed genetically to offspring
option_c: Are acquired through learning, repetition, and experience (as demonstrated by Pavlov's dog)
option_d: Occur independently of sensory receptors and motor effectors
explanation: Ivan Pavlov showed that conditioned reflexes are learned behavioral responses established when an indifferent stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus.
subject: Biology

question: The part of the mammalian brain responsible for intelligence, conscious thought, memory, and voluntary movement is the:
option_a: Cerebellum
option_b: Medulla oblongata
option_c: Pons Varolii
option_d: Cerebrum (cerebral cortex)
explanation: The cerebrum is the largest brain region; its folded cortex mediates higher intellectual functions, conscious perception, sensory interpretation, and voluntary motor output.
subject: Biology

question: The cerebellum plays a vital role in:
option_a: Coordinating muscle movements, maintaining posture, and bodily balance
option_b: Regulating heart rate and respiratory rhythms
option_c: Secretory control of thyroid and adrenal hormones
option_d: Generating emotional anger and aggression impulses
explanation: The cerebellum coordinates complex voluntary movements, smooths muscle contractions, and preserves balance, posture, and equilibrium.
subject: Biology

question: Vital involuntary vegetative functions, such as cardiac rate, blood pressure, peristalsis, and breathing, are controlled by the:
option_a: Corpus callosum
option_b: Medulla oblongata
option_c: Thalamus
option_d: Optic chiasma
explanation: The medulla oblongata at the base of the brainstem contains autonomic reflex centres governing cardiac activity, vasomotor tone, respiration, swallowing, and vomiting.
subject: Biology

question: The hypothalamus functions as an essential bridge between the nervous system and endocrine system by controlling the:
option_a: Adrenal cortex
option_b: Thyroid gland
option_c: Pituitary gland
option_d: Parathyroid glands
explanation: The hypothalamus integrates neuro-endocrine signaling; it synthesizes releasing and inhibiting hormones that regulate anterior pituitary secretion.
subject: Biology

question: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is divided into two functionally opposing divisions termed the:
option_a: Somatic and Central nervous systems
option_b: Cranial and Spinal cord networks
option_c: Sensory and Motor peripheral pathways
option_d: Sympathetic and Parasympathetic nervous systems
explanation: The ANS comprises the sympathetic division ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic division ('rest and digest'), exerting antagonistic control over viscera.
subject: Biology

question: Activation of the sympathetic nervous system during an emergency produces which physiological response?
option_a: Dilation of pupils, increased heart rate, and inhibition of digestion
option_b: Constriction of pupils, decreased heart rate, and stimulation of peristalsis
option_c: Increased glycogen synthesis and insulin secretion by the pancreas
option_d: Constriction of bronchioles and lowering of arterial blood pressure
explanation: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for stress: accelerating heart rate, dilating bronchioles and pupils, and diverting blood away from the digestive tract.
subject: Biology

question: The meninges are the three protective membranes that envelop the brain and spinal cord; from outermost to innermost, they are the:
option_a: Pia mater, Arachnoid mater, and Dura mater
option_b: Dura mater, Arachnoid mater, and Pia mater
option_c: Pericardium, Pleura, and Peritoneum
option_d: Cornea, Sclera, and Choroid layer
explanation: The meninges protect the CNS: outer tough fibrous Dura mater, middle web-like Arachnoid mater, and inner vascular Pia mater adhering to the nervous tissue.
subject: Biology

question: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cushions the brain and spinal cord from mechanical shock and is found circulating within the:
option_a: Epidural space between skull and scalp
option_b: Central canal of the bone osteon
option_c: Subarachnoid space and brain ventricles
option_d: Coronary sulcus of the left ventricle
explanation: CSF is produced by choroid plexuses in brain ventricles and circulates in the subarachnoid space and central spinal canal, providing mechanical buoyancy.
subject: Biology

question: A sensory neuron is characterized morphologically by possessing a:
option_a: Short dendron and multipolar axon terminating in a skeletal motor endplate
option_b: Complete absence of axon terminals and myelin coverings
option_c: Nucleus located within the ventral horn gray matter of the spinal cord
option_d: Cell body located in the dorsal root ganglion with a long dendron
explanation: Sensory (afferent) neurons are pseudo-unipolar; their soma resides in the dorsal root ganglion, possessing a long peripheral dendron and axon entering the cord.
subject: Biology

question: Multiple sclerosis is a debilitating neurological disorder caused by:
option_a: Autoimmune destruction of the myelin sheath in the central nervous system
option_b: Excessive production of cerebrospinal fluid causing hydrocephalus
option_c: Bacterial infection of the pituitary infundibulum stalk
option_d: Hypertrophy of the cerebellar Purkinje cell dendrites
explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease where the body's immune system attacks and degrades myelin in the CNS, impairing nerve impulse conduction.
subject: Biology

question: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the human eye that contains photoreceptor cells is the:
option_a: Choroid
option_b: Retina
option_c: Sclera
option_d: Cornea
explanation: The retina is the innermost nervous tunic of the eyeball containing light-detecting rod and cone photoreceptors.
subject: Biology

question: In the human retina, rod cells are specialized for:
option_a: Detailed sharp vision and vibrant colour perception in bright light
option_b: Refracting incoming light rays directly onto the optic nerve disc
option_c: Vision in dim light (scotopic vision) and detecting black and white shades
option_d: Secreting watery aqueous humor into the anterior chamber
explanation: Rods contain the photopigment rhodopsin; they are sensitive to low light intensities (night vision) but cannot distinguish colors.
subject: Biology

question: Cone cells in the retina are concentrated most densely in the:
option_a: Blind spot (optic disc)
option_b: Anterior ciliary zonule
option_c: Ora serrata margin
option_d: Fovea centralis (yellow spot / macula lutea)
explanation: The fovea centralis consists entirely of tightly packed cone cells, providing maximum visual acuity and rich color discrimination.
subject: Biology

question: The transparent front portion of the eye's fibrous coat that carries out the greatest refraction of incoming light is the:
option_a: Cornea
option_b: Pupil
option_c: Crystalline lens
option_d: Vitreous humor
explanation: The curved anterior surface of the cornea accounts for roughly two-thirds of the eye's total optical refractive power.
subject: Biology

question: Accommodation of the human eye for focusing on near objects involves:
option_a: Relaxation of ciliary muscles, tightening of suspensory ligaments, and flattening of the lens
option_b: Contraction of ciliary muscles, loosening of suspensory ligaments, and lens becoming more convex
option_c: Complete closure of the pupil by circular iris muscles
option_d: Movement of the entire eyeball backward into the bony orbit
explanation: For near vision, ciliary muscles contract, relaxing suspensory ligaments; the elastic lens rounds up (becomes more convex), increasing its refractive power.
subject: Biology

question: Myopia (short-sightedness) occurs when the eyeball is too long or lens too curved, causing distant images to focus in front of the retina. It is corrected using a:
option_a: Convex (converging) lens
option_b: Cylindrical lens
option_c: Concave (diverging) lens
option_d: Bifocal magnifying prism
explanation: A concave lens diverges incoming parallel light rays before they hit the eye, pushing the focal point back onto the retina.
subject: Biology

question: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is corrected using a:
option_a: Concave (diverging) lens
option_b: Plano-concave lens
option_c: Tinted polarized filter
option_d: Convex (converging) lens
explanation: In hypermetropia, light from nearby objects focuses behind the retina; a convex lens converges light rays to focus sharply on the retina.
subject: Biology

question: Astigmatism is an optical defect of the eye caused by:
option_a: Uneven curvature of the cornea or crystalline lens
option_b: Gradual opacity and clouding of the lens with age
option_c: Loss of elasticity of the lens capsule in elderly persons
option_d: Absence of cone cells in the peripheral retina
explanation: Astigmatism results from irregular, non-spherical curvature of the cornea or lens, preventing rays in different planes from focusing at a single point; it is corrected with cylindrical lenses.
subject: Biology

question: The blind spot in the human eye corresponds to the region where:
option_a: The retinal artery and vein are completely absent
option_b: The optic nerve exits the eyeball and no photoreceptor rods or cones exist
option_c: Vitreous humor is replaced by pressurized aqueous fluid
option_d: Ciliary muscle fibers attach to the choroid coat
explanation: The optic disc (blind spot) lacks rods and cones because axons of ganglion cells converge here to form the optic nerve, creating an insensitive visual spot.
subject: Biology

question: The three small auditory ossicles in the mammalian middle ear, in order from tympanic membrane to oval window, are the:
option_a: Stapes, Malleus, and Incus
option_b: Incus, Stapes, and Malleus
option_c: Malleus (hammer), Incus (anvil), and Stapes (stirrup)
option_d: Cochlea, Utricle, and Saccule
explanation: The middle ear ossicles form a mechanical lever system bridging the tympanum and oval window: Malleus → Incus → Stapes.
subject: Biology

question: The primary organ of hearing located within the inner ear's cochlea is the:
option_a: Semicircular canal cupula
option_b: Ampullary crista
option_c: Macula of the utricle
option_d: Organ of Corti
explanation: The Organ of Corti rests on the basilar membrane in the cochlea; its specialized hair cells transduce fluid vibrations into auditory nerve impulses.
subject: Biology

question: Maintenance of dynamic body balance and detection of rotational head movements is performed by the:
option_a: Semicircular canals (ampullae)
option_b: Cochlear duct
option_c: Eustachian tube
option_d: Tympanic membrane
explanation: The three fluid-filled semicircular canals arranged at right angles detect angular rotational acceleration via hair cells in their ampullary cristae.
subject: Biology

question: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the nasopharynx to:
option_a: Drain excess perilymph fluid into the salivary glands
option_b: Equalize air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane (eardrum)
option_c: Conduct sound waves directly into the auditory cortex
option_d: Amplify high-frequency sound waves entering the pinna
explanation: The Eustachian tube balances atmospheric pressure on either side of the eardrum, preventing tympanic rupture during altitude or pressure changes.
subject: Biology

question: Which receptor in mammalian skin is specialized for detecting deep pressure and high-frequency vibration?
option_a: Meissner's corpuscle
option_b: Merkel disc
option_c: Pacinian corpuscle
option_d: Free nerve ending
explanation: Pacinian (lamellar) corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors located deep in the dermis and hypodermis that respond to deep pressure and vibration.
subject: Biology

question: Temperature regulation by the skin in cold environments involves:
option_a: Vasodilation of dermal arterioles and profuse perspiration from sweat pores
option_b: Increased secretion of oily sebum from sebaceous glands
option_c: Rapid shedding of stratum corneum dead epidermal scales
option_d: Vasoconstriction of dermal blood vessels and contraction of arrector pili muscles (erect hairs)
explanation: In the cold, sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood away from the skin surface to minimize heat loss, while arrector pili muscles contract (goosebumps).
subject: Biology

question: Hormones are chemical messengers synthesized by:
option_a: Ductless endocrine glands and secreted directly into the bloodstream
option_b: Exocrine glands with specialized ducts discharging onto body surfaces
option_c: Skeletal muscle fibers during anaerobic lactic acid synthesis
option_d: Glial astrocytes in cerebral cerebrospinal fluid
explanation: Endocrine glands lack ducts; they release hormones directly into interstitial fluid and the bloodstream to exert regulatory effects on target organs.
subject: Biology

question: The 'master gland' of the endocrine system that controls the secretion of many other endocrine glands is the:
option_a: Thyroid gland
option_b: Pituitary gland (hypophysis)
option_c: Pancreas
option_d: Adrenal gland
explanation: The anterior pituitary secretes trophic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, GH) that direct and stimulate downstream endocrine glands.
subject: Biology

question: Insulin is a polypeptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas that functions to:
option_a: Stimulate the breakdown of hepatic glycogen into free glucose
option_b: Convert amino acids into fatty acids during starvation
option_c: Lower blood glucose levels by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis
option_d: Accelerate the ultrafiltration rate of blood in renal glomeruli
explanation: Insulin facilitates cellular glucose uptake (via GLUT4 translocation) and promotes glycogenesis in the liver and muscles, reducing blood sugar.
subject: Biology

question: Glucagon is secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets and functions antagonistically to insulin by:
option_a: Inhibiting the breakdown of lipids in adipose adipose stores
option_b: Promoting the reabsorption of calcium ions in distal renal tubules
option_c: Lowering metabolic basal heat production during cold weather
option_d: Stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver to raise blood sugar
explanation: Glucagon elevates low blood glucose by stimulating the liver to hydrolyze glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and synthesize glucose from lactate/amino acids.
subject: Biology

question: Thyroxine (T4) is secreted by the thyroid gland and requires which essential trace dietary element for its synthesis?
option_a: Iodine
option_b: Iron
option_c: Cobalt
option_d: Zinc
explanation: Iodine is an essential constituent of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); dietary iodine deficiency causes compensatory thyroid enlargement (endemic goiter).
subject: Biology

question: A deficiency of thyroxine during infancy leads to a developmental disorder characterized by stunted physical and mental growth known as:
option_a: Gigantism
option_b: Cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism)
option_c: Acromegaly
option_d: Cushing's syndrome
explanation: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism in infants causes cretinism, resulting in severe irreversible intellectual impairment, dwarfism, and skeletal abnormalities.
subject: Biology

question: Adrenaline (epinephrine), the 'fight or flight' hormone, is secreted by the:
option_a: Adrenal cortex
option_b: Parathyroid gland
option_c: Adrenal medulla
option_d: Thymus gland
explanation: The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline in response to acute stress, elevating heart rate, blood pressure, and blood sugar.
subject: Biology

question: Which hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex regulates sodium and potassium electrolyte balance in the body?
option_a: Cortisol
option_b: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
option_c: Vasopressin
option_d: Aldosterone
explanation: Aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid) stimulates sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts of nephrons.
subject: Biology

question: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates blood calcium homeostasis by:
option_a: Increasing blood calcium levels through bone resorption and calcium reabsorption in kidneys
option_b: Lowering blood calcium by stimulating osteoblast bone mineralization
option_c: Promoting the excretion of ionic calcium through sweat glands
option_d: Inhibiting the activation of vitamin D in renal proximal tubules
explanation: PTH elevates ionized calcium in the blood by stimulating osteoclasts to dissolve bone matrix, enhancing renal Ca2+ reabsorption, and activating vitamin D.
subject: Biology

question: Calcitonin is a thyroid hormone that works antagonistically to parathyroid hormone (PTH) by:
option_a: Stimulating osteoclasts to dissolve trabecular bone lamellae
option_b: Lowering blood calcium concentration and promoting calcium deposition in bones
option_c: Increasing intestinal absorption of dietary calcium cations
option_d: Inducing the immediate excretion of magnesium ions in bile
explanation: Calcitonin (secreted by parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid) reduces blood calcium levels by inhibiting osteoclasts and stimulating bone mineralization.
subject: Biology

question: Growth hormone (somatotropin) hypersecretion during childhood results in:
option_a: Dwarfism
option_b: Acromegaly
option_c: Gigantism
option_d: Myxedema
explanation: Excess growth hormone before epiphyseal plates fuse in long bones causes accelerated vertical bone growth, resulting in gigantism.
subject: Biology

question: Acromegaly is an endocrine condition that occurs when:
option_a: Thyroid stimulating hormone is chronically deficient from birth
option_b: Insulin production ceases entirely due to autoimmune beta cell destruction
option_c: Cortisol levels drop precipitously following bilateral adrenalectomy
option_d: Growth hormone is hypersecreted in adulthood after the epiphyseal plates have fused
explanation: In adults, excess GH cannot lengthen long bones; instead, it causes abnormal bone thickening and soft tissue enlargement of the face, hands, and feet (acromegaly).
subject: Biology

question: Homeostasis is maintained primarily through which physiological mechanism?
option_a: Negative feedback loops
option_b: Continuous positive runaway amplification
option_c: Passive gravitational drainage
option_d: Periodic cellular apoptosis cycles
explanation: Negative feedback loops detect deviations from a biological set point and trigger counter-responses that reverse the change back toward the baseline.
subject: Biology

question: When body core temperature rises above the normal set point (37°C), the thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus initiates:
option_a: Involuntary shivering of skeletal postural muscle groups
option_b: Vasodilation of cutaneous arterioles and activation of eccrine sweat glands
option_c: Secretion of high levels of thyroxine and adrenaline
option_d: Piloerection of body hairs through arrector pili contraction
explanation: To cool down, the hypothalamus triggers cutaneous vasodilation (radiating heat) and activates sweat glands (cooling via evaporative heat loss).
subject: Biology

question: Which of the following hormones stimulates uterine contractions during human labour and milk ejection during breastfeeding?
option_a: Prolactin
option_b: Progesterone
option_c: Oxytocin
option_d: Estrogen
explanation: Oxytocin (from the posterior pituitary) stimulates myometrial contractions during childbirth (positive feedback) and contraction of myoepithelial cells for milk letdown.
subject: Biology

question: Asexual reproduction involves:
option_a: The union of male and female haploid gametic nuclei
option_b: Compulsory meiotic recombination in reproductive gonads
option_c: The cross-pollination of floral stigma surfaces
option_d: A single parent producing offspring without the fusion of gametes
explanation: Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring (clones) from a single parent through mitotic cell divisions, without gamete fusion.
subject: Biology

question: Binary fission is the primary mode of asexual reproduction in:
option_a: Amoeba and bacteria
option_b: Hydra and yeast
option_c: Flowering dicotyledonous shrubs
option_d: Tapeworms and liver flukes
explanation: In binary fission, a single unicellular organism replicates its DNA and divides equally into two genetically identical daughter cells (e.g. Amoeba, bacteria).
subject: Biology

question: Budding is an asexual reproductive process observed in:
option_a: Spirogyra and Chlamydomonas
option_b: Yeast and Hydra
option_c: Ferns and mosses
option_d: Houseflies and honeybees
explanation: In budding (e.g. yeast, Hydra), a localized cellular outgrowth (bud) develops on the parent body, matures, and eventually detaches as an independent organism.
subject: Biology

question: Multiple fission (schizogony) occurs in which parasitic organism inside human liver and red blood cells?
option_a: Trypanosoma brucei
option_b: Entamoeba histolytica
option_c: Plasmodium (malaria parasite)
option_d: Schistosoma mansoni
explanation: Plasmodium undergoes schizogony (multiple fission), where the nucleus divides repeatedly before cytoplasmic cleavage, producing multiple merozoites.
subject: Biology

question: Fragmentation as a method of asexual reproduction is characteristic of:
option_a: Mucor
option_b: Paramecium
option_c: Euglena
option_d: Spirogyra
explanation: In Spirogyra, accidental breakage or mechanical shearing of the filamentous alga into fragments results in each piece growing into a new filament by mitosis.
subject: Biology

question: Spore formation in the black bread mould (Rhizopus stolonifer) takes place inside specialized structures called:
option_a: Sporangia
option_b: Basidia
option_c: Antheridia
option_d: Archegonia
explanation: Rhizopus produces erect aerial hyphae (sporangiophores) bearing swollen black spherical capsules (sporangia) packed with asexual haploid spores.
subject: Biology

question: Vegetative propagation in flowering plants refers to the development of new plants from:
option_a: Floral petals and stamens following fertilization
option_b: Vegetative organs such as roots, stems, and leaves
option_c: Haploid microspores released from mature anthers
option_d: Diploid zygotic embryos encased within fruit carpels
explanation: Vegetative propagation is the asexual generation of new plants from vegetative structures (stems, leaves, roots, tubers, bulbs, runners).
subject: Biology

question: Which of the following plants reproduces vegetatively using adventitious foliar buds along its leaf margins?
option_a: Ginger (Zingiber officinale)
option_b: Irish potato (Solanum tuberosum)
option_c: Bryophyllum (miracle leaf)
option_d: Onion (Allium cepa)
explanation: Bryophyllum bears notch buds along leaf serrations that develop roots and miniature plantlets, which detach and root in soil.
subject: Biology

question: The underground vegetative reproductive organ of the onion (Allium cepa) is a:
option_a: Stem tuber bearing eye buds
option_b: Horizontal fleshy rhizome
option_c: Vertical solid corm
option_d: Bulb (consisting of fleshy scale leaves and a condensed basal stem)
explanation: An onion is a tunicated bulb consisting of a flattened discoid stem surrounded by concentric fleshy storage leaves (scales) enclosing a central apical bud.
subject: Biology

question: Irish potato (Solanum tuberosum) propagates vegetatively by means of underground:
option_a: Stem tubers possessing 'eyes' (lateral buds)
option_b: Swollen adventitious root tubers
option_c: Surface horizontal runners (stolons)
option_d: Sub-aerial suckers with terminal rosettes
explanation: Irish potato tubers are swollen underground stem ends; the 'eyes' are nodes containing axillary buds capable of sprouting into new aerial shoots.
subject: Biology

question: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) propagates asexually through an underground horizontal stem termed a:
option_a: Corm
option_b: Rhizome
option_c: Runner
option_d: Tuber
explanation: A rhizome is a horizontal underground storage stem with nodes, internodes, scaly leaves, and axillary buds that sprout into new plants.
subject: Biology

question: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) differs botanically from Irish potato because sweet potato is a swollen:
option_a: Stem tuber
option_b: Foliar bulb
option_c: Root tuber
option_d: Underground corm
explanation: Sweet potato is a modified adventitious storage root (root tuber), whereas Irish potato is a modified underground stem (stem tuber).
subject: Biology

question: Grafting and budding are artificial vegetative propagation techniques that involve joining a:
option_a: Pollen grain onto an unfertilized ovule
option_b: Cotyledon onto an emerging radicle tip
option_c: Petiole onto a photosynthetic leaf blade
option_d: Scion (upper bud/shoot) onto a Rootstock (rooted lower stem)
explanation: Grafting joins a detached shoot/bud possessing desirable traits (the scion) onto the established root system of another plant (the stock) to grow as one.
subject: Biology

question: A major commercial advantage of vegetative propagation over sexual reproduction from seeds is that:
option_a: Offspring retain exact parental characteristics and mature much faster
option_b: It generates wide genetic variability and new hybrids
option_c: It eliminates all transmission of viral systemic plant diseases
option_d: Seeds can be stored dry for decades in grain silos
explanation: Vegetative propagation preserves elite genetic traits without segregation, produces uniform crops, and yields harvests faster than growing from seed.
subject: Biology

question: Parthenogenesis is an unusual reproductive mode where an offspring develops from a(n):
option_a: Enucleated somatic cell fused with a bacterial plasmid
option_b: Unfertilized female egg cell without sperm fertilization (e.g. drone honeybees)
option_c: Mitotic division of an unreduced pollen mother cell
option_d: Fusion of two male spermatozoa inside the oviduct
explanation: Parthenogenesis is reproduction from an unfertilized ovum (e.g. in aphids, male drone bees, and some whiptail lizards).
subject: Biology

question: The female reproductive organ of a flowering plant is the:
option_a: Stamen (androecium)
option_b: Corolla (petals)
option_c: Pistil (carpel / gynoecium)
option_d: Calyx (sepals)
explanation: The pistil (carpel) is the female organ composed of the stigma (receptive surface), style (neck), and ovary (containing ovules).
subject: Biology

question: The male reproductive unit of a flower (stamen) consists of the:
option_a: Stigma and style
option_b: Ovary and ovule
option_c: Sepal and receptacle
option_d: Anther and filament
explanation: The stamen consists of a slender stalk (filament) supporting a pollen-bearing head (anther) containing four microsporangia.
subject: Biology

question: Pollination is biologically defined as the transfer of pollen grains from the:
option_a: Anther to the receptive stigma of a flower
option_b: Stigma to the micropyle of an ovule
option_c: Filament to the floral nectary gland
option_d: Pollen tube to the diploid polar nuclei
explanation: Pollination is the mechanical transfer of pollen from the dehiscing anther to the receptive stigma of the same or another flower.
subject: Biology

question: Wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flowers are typically characterized by having:
option_a: Large brightly coloured petals, strong sweet scents, and sticky nectar
option_b: Small inconspicuous petals, feathery stigmas, and large quantities of light, dry pollen
option_c: Heavy sticky pollen grains and short non-protruding anthers
option_d: Deep nectar spurs that conceal floral secretory glands
explanation: Anemophilous flowers lack showy petals/scent, producing abundant buoyant pollen and expansive feathery stigmas to catch airborne grains.
subject: Biology

question: Insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers attract pollinators through:
option_a: Pendulous catkins that dangle exposed in strong wind gusts
option_b: Smooth, non-sticky pollen grains that drift in air currents
option_c: Brightly coloured petals, sweet floral scents, and sugary nectar
option_d: Dull greenish perianths lacking all nectaries
explanation: Entomophilous flowers feature conspicuous colorful corollas, pleasant fragrances, nectar rewards, and rough, spiny pollen that clings to insect bodies.
subject: Biology

question: Self-pollination occurs when pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma of:
option_a: A flower on a different plant of the same species
option_b: A flower belonging to an entirely unrelated botanical family
option_c: A non-angiospermous pine cone scale
option_d: The same flower or another flower on the exact same plant
explanation: Self-pollination (autogamy/geitonogamy) is the transfer of pollen to a stigma of the same flower or another flower on the identical plant.
subject: Biology

question: Dichogamy is an adaptation that prevents self-pollination in bisexual flowers by ensuring that:
option_a: Anthers and stigmas mature at different times
option_b: The styles are much longer than the stamen filaments
option_c: Male and female flowers occur on separate individual plants
option_d: Pollen grains fail to germinate on stigmas of the same flower
explanation: Dichogamy is temporal separation in the maturation of male and female floral organs: protandry (anthers mature first) or protogyny (stigmas mature first).
subject: Biology

question: Protandry is a mechanism promoting cross-pollination where:
option_a: The stigma matures and withers before the anthers release pollen
option_b: The anthers shed their pollen before the stigma of the same flower becomes receptive
option_c: The petals remain permanently closed to exclude insects
option_d: The ovules abort whenever self-pollen lands on the stigma
explanation: In protandrous flowers (e.g. sunflower, maize), pollen is shed before the stigma matures, preventing self-fertilization.
subject: Biology

question: Dioecious plants enforce cross-pollination because:
option_a: Both stamens and carpels are housed inside the same floral envelope
option_b: Pollen tubes take three weeks to reach the embryo sac
option_c: Male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers are borne on separate individual plants
option_d: Flowers open strictly at night and close by dawn
explanation: In dioecious species (e.g. pawpaw, date palm), individual plants are strictly male or strictly female, making self-pollination physically impossible.
subject: Biology

question: Double fertilization is a unique phenomenon characteristic of angiosperms in which:
option_a: Two separate pollen grains penetrate the exact same ovule simultaneously
option_b: The generative nucleus divides twice to produce four haploid embryos
option_c: Both the calyx and corolla develop into succulent edible fruit flesh
option_d: One sperm nucleus fertilizes the egg cell (forming a diploid zygote) while the other fuses with two polar nuclei (forming triploid endosperm)
explanation: Double fertilization involves two sperm cells: one fuses with the ovum to form the 2n zygote; the second fuses with 2 polar nuclei to form 3n endosperm tissue.
subject: Biology

question: The triploid (3n) endosperm in an angiosperm seed functions primarily to:
option_a: Provide nutritive food reserves for the developing embryo
option_b: Form the tough protective outer seed coat (testa)
option_c: Direct the geotropic curvature of the emerging radicle
option_d: Synthesize chlorophyll before seedling germination
explanation: The triploid endosperm tissue stores carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids to nourish the growing embryo during seed development and germination.
subject: Biology

question: Following successful fertilization in a flowering plant, the ovary develops into the:
option_a: Seed
option_b: Fruit
option_c: Testa
option_d: Micropyle
explanation: Following fertilization, hormonal signals induce the ovary wall (pericarp) to enlarge and mature into a fruit enclosing the seeds.
subject: Biology

question: Following fertilization, the ovule inside the angiosperm ovary matures into the:
option_a: Fruit
option_b: Pericarp
option_c: Seed
option_d: Receptacle
explanation: The fertilized and matured ovule forms the seed, with its integuments hardening to become the seed coat (testa).
subject: Biology

question: The micropyle of a mature dicot seed (such as a cowpea seed) functions as a minute pore through which:
option_a: Manufactured sucrose is translocated from leaves
option_b: Excess carbon dioxide is pumped out during dormancy
option_c: Pollen tubes escape after double fertilization
option_d: Water and oxygen enter the seed during germination
explanation: The micropyle is a small pore in the seed coat through which water and oxygen enter to imbibe the cotyledons and initiate germination.
subject: Biology

question: Epigeal germination is distinguished from hypogeal germination because in epigeal germination:
option_a: The hypocotyl elongates rapidly, carrying the cotyledons above the soil surface
option_b: The epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons remain below ground
option_c: The seed embryo fails to develop an emerging primary radicle
option_d: Photosynthesis takes place underground inside the endosperm
explanation: In epigeal germination (e.g. bean, castor oil), the hypocotyl elongates, arching upward and pulling the cotyledons above the soil into sunlight.
subject: Biology

question: The primary male reproductive organ responsible for spermatogenesis and testosterone synthesis is the:
option_a: Prostate gland
option_b: Testis
option_c: Epididymis
option_d: Seminal vesicle
explanation: The testes contain seminiferous tubules that produce spermatozoa and interstitial Leydig cells that secrete testosterone.
subject: Biology

question: Human testes are housed externally in the scrotum primarily because:
option_a: The scrotum protects developing sperm cells from atmospheric ultraviolet light
option_b: Urinary excretion would contaminate the semen inside the abdominal cavity
option_c: Spermatogenesis requires a temperature 2 to 3°C lower than normal core body temperature
option_d: Testicular Leydig cells require direct exposure to environmental air
explanation: Viable sperm production requires temperatures 2–3°C below core body temperature; the scrotum regulates temperature through the dartos and cremaster muscles.
subject: Biology

question: Spermatozoa undergo maturation and temporary storage within the coiled structure called the:
option_a: Vas deferens
option_b: Prostate gland
option_c: Urethra
option_d: Epididymis
explanation: Sperm cells exiting the seminiferous tubules enter the epididymis where they spend roughly two weeks maturing and acquiring motility.
subject: Biology

question: The cutting and tying of the vas deferens (sperm ducts) as a permanent method of male surgical sterilization is called:
option_a: Vasectomy
option_b: Tubal ligation
option_c: Laparoscopy
option_d: Circumcision
explanation: Vasectomy is a surgical contraceptive procedure that severs or seals the vasa deferentia, preventing sperm from entering the ejaculatory duct.
subject: Biology

question: Which male accessory gland secretes an alkaline fluid rich in fructose to nourish motile spermatozoa?
option_a: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands
option_b: Seminal vesicles
option_c: Thyroid gland
option_d: Adrenal medulla
explanation: The paired seminal vesicles produce an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that constitutes about 60–70% of semen volume, providing energy for sperm motility.
subject: Biology

question: The site of human oogenesis and secretion of estrogen and progesterone is the:
option_a: Uterus
option_b: Fallopian tube
option_c: Ovary
option_d: Cervix
explanation: The ovaries produce female gametes (ova) within developing ovarian follicles and synthesize the steroid sex hormones estrogen and progesterone.
subject: Biology

question: Fertilization of the human ovum by a spermatozoon typically takes place in the:
option_a: Uterine endometrial cavity
option_b: Cervical canal
option_c: Ovarian Graafian follicle
option_d: Fallopian tube (oviduct / ampulla)
explanation: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla region of the Fallopian tube (oviduct) when a sperm successfully penetrates the secondary oocyte.
subject: Biology

question: The surge of which pituitary hormone directly triggers ovulation (the release of a mature ovum from the Graafian follicle)?
option_a: Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
option_b: Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
option_c: Prolactin
option_d: Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
explanation: A sharp mid-cycle surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) induced by high estrogen triggers the rupture of the mature follicle and release of the egg (ovulation).
subject: Biology

question: Following ovulation, the ruptured Graafian follicle transforms into a temporary endocrine structure called the:
option_a: Corpus albicans
option_b: Corpus luteum
option_c: Blastocyst
option_d: Trophoblast
explanation: The collapsed follicle reorganizes into the corpus luteum, which secretes high levels of progesterone to maintain the uterine lining for implantation.
subject: Biology

question: Progesterone maintains pregnancy primarily by:
option_a: Stimulating the pituitary gland to secrete high levels of FSH and LH
option_b: Inducing the immediate breakdown and shedding of the myometrium
option_c: Thickening and vascularizing the uterine endometrium and inhibiting uterine contractions
option_d: Accelerating the maturation of new Graafian follicles in the ovary
explanation: Progesterone prepares the endometrium for blastocyst implantation, maintains its vascular structure, and suppresses uterine muscle contractions during gestation.
subject: Biology

question: Implantation in human reproduction refers to the process where the:
option_a: Spermatozoon penetrates the outer corona radiata of the secondary oocyte
option_b: Secondary oocyte bursts forth from the surface of the mature ovary
option_c: Placenta separates from the myometrium following childbirth
option_d: Blastocyst attaches and embeds into the vascular endometrial lining of the uterus
explanation: About 6 to 7 days after fertilization, the developing blastocyst embeds itself into the receptive endometrium of the uterus (implantation).
subject: Biology

question: The primary organ through which exchange of nutrients, respiratory gases, and wastes occurs between mother and fetus is the:
option_a: Placenta
option_b: Amnion
option_c: Yolk sac
option_d: Allantois
explanation: The placenta facilitates diffusion of oxygen, glucose, and amino acids from maternal blood to fetal blood and transfers fetal CO2 and urea to the mother.
subject: Biology

question: Why is it biologically vital that maternal and fetal blood do not mix directly across the placenta?
option_a: Because fetal blood contains no red hemoglobin respiratory pigments
option_b: To prevent destruction of fetal erythrocytes by maternal antibodies and buffer against high maternal blood pressure
option_c: Because maternal blood is toxic to all eukaryotic mammalian tissues
option_d: To allow the fetus to maintain an entirely distinct atmospheric body temperature
explanation: Direct mixing could trigger catastrophic agglutination if ABO or Rh groups conflict, and high maternal arterial pressure would rupture delicate fetal capillaries.
subject: Biology

question: The fluid-filled sac that encloses the developing embryo and cushions it against mechanical shocks and trauma is the:
option_a: Chorion
option_b: Allantoic stalk
option_c: Amnion (containing amniotic fluid)
option_d: Umbilical cord
explanation: The amnion encloses the fetus in amniotic fluid, which cushions against physical jolts, maintains uniform temperature, and allows fetal movement.
subject: Biology

question: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta and contains:
option_a: Two umbilical veins carrying deoxygenated blood and one umbilical artery
option_b: One single muscular artery and no venous blood vessels
option_c: A bundle of motor and sensory spinal nerves embedded in keratin
option_d: Two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood and one umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood
explanation: The umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries (carrying fetal metabolic wastes and deoxygenated blood to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood to the fetus).
subject: Biology

question: Menstruation (the shedding of the uterine lining and unfertilized ovum) occurs when:
option_a: Progesterone and estrogen levels drop sharply due to degeneration of the corpus luteum
option_b: Luteinizing hormone levels surge to their peak concentration
option_c: Human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the ovarian cortex
option_d: The endometrial capillaries expand under elevated blood pressure
explanation: If fertilization fails, the corpus luteum degenerates into the corpus albicans; the sharp drop in progesterone causes endometrial ischemia and shedding.
subject: Biology

question: The acrosome located at the anterior tip of the mammalian sperm head contains:
option_a: Numerous ATP-generating mitochondria for flagellar swimming propulsion
option_b: Hydrolytic enzymes (like hyaluronidase) that digest the protective coats of the ovum
option_c: The haploid maternal chromosomes arranged in bivalents
option_d: A large nutrient glycogen reserve to feed the zygote
explanation: The acrosome is a modified lysosome containing digestive enzymes that break down the zona pellucida and corona radiata, enabling fertilization.
subject: Biology

question: Which of the following hormones is detected in the urine of a pregnant woman by modern home pregnancy test kits?
option_a: Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH)
option_b: Prolactin
option_c: Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
option_d: Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)
explanation: Trophoblast cells of the implanted blastocyst secrete hCG, which prevents corpus luteum degeneration; hCG excreted in urine is detected by pregnancy tests.
subject: Biology

question: Surgical tying and cutting of the Fallopian tubes in a woman to achieve permanent contraception is called:
option_a: Hysterectomy
option_b: Oophorectomy
option_c: Amniocentesis
option_d: Tubal ligation
explanation: Tubal ligation blocks or severs the Fallopian tubes, preventing released ova from meeting sperm and achieving permanent surgical contraception.
subject: Biology

question: Identical (monozygotic) twins result when:
option_a: A single fertilized ovum splits into two separate embryos during early cleavage
option_b: Two separate ova are ovulated and fertilized by two different spermatozoa
option_c: A single ovum is fertilized simultaneously by two distinct sperm cells
option_d: Two blastocysts fuse together inside the fallopian ampulla
explanation: Monozygotic twins develop when a single zygote divides into two independent cell masses during early cleavage, resulting in identical genetic makeups and same sex.
subject: Biology

question: Growth in multicellular living organisms involves which of the following irreversible processes?
option_a: Temporary enlargement due to passive absorption of water molecules
option_b: Permanent increase in size, dry mass, and complexity accompanied by cell division and differentiation
option_c: Periodic fluctuations in weight during alternating seasons
option_d: The accumulation of inert non-living mineral crystals on epidermal surfaces
explanation: Biological growth is defined as a permanent, irreversible increase in dry mass, size, and cell number through mitotic divisions and cellular differentiation.
subject: Biology

question: Plant growth differs fundamentally from animal growth because plant growth is:
option_a: Uniformly distributed throughout all somatic body organs and tissues
option_b: Limited strictly to a juvenile developmental phase before stopping completely
option_c: Localized at specific growing regions (meristems) and indeterminate (continues throughout life)
option_d: Dependent on the intake of preformed organic animal proteins
explanation: Plants exhibit localized apical and lateral meristematic growth that can continue indefinitely, whereas animals exhibit diffuse, determinate growth.
subject: Biology

question: The region of actively dividing undifferentiated cells located at the growing tips of roots and shoots is the:
option_a: Vascular cambium
option_b: Cork cambium (phellogen)
option_c: Endodermis layer
option_d: Apical meristem
explanation: Apical meristems at root and shoot apices divide mitotically, driving primary growth and longitudinal elongation of plant organs.
subject: Biology

question: Secondary growth in dicotyledonous woody stems results in increased girth (thickness) and is caused by the activity of the:
option_a: Vascular cambium and cork cambium (lateral meristems)
option_b: Apical meristems and intercalary nodes
option_c: Protoderm and ground meristematic parenchyma
option_d: Collenchyma thickenings and root hair expansions
explanation: Lateral meristems (vascular cambium producing secondary xylem/phloem and cork cambium producing bark) produce secondary thickening in woody dicots.
subject: Biology

question: An auxanometer is a laboratory instrument used to measure the:
option_a: Rate of transpiration in leafy mesophytes
option_b: Rate of growth in plant shoots or roots
option_c: Volume of oxygen gas evolved during photosynthesis
option_d: Intensity of osmotic pressure inside xylem vessels
explanation: An auxanometer (arc or lever auxanometer) magnifies and measures minute increments in the longitudinal growth rate of plant stems.
subject: Biology

question: A classic sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve consists of which sequence of phases?
option_a: Stationary phase → Lag phase → Exponential phase → Death phase
option_b: Log phase → Lag phase → Linear phase → Plateau phase
option_c: Lag phase → Exponential (log) phase → Decelerating phase → Stationary (plateau) phase
option_d: Plateau phase → Accelerating phase → Exponential phase → Decline phase
explanation: A typical sigmoid growth curve displays: Lag phase (slow initial growth), Log phase (exponential rapid growth), Deceleration phase, and Stationary plateau.
subject: Biology

question: Metamorphosis in insects refers to the:
option_a: Periodic shedding of cuticular scales during daily flight
option_b: Conversion of vegetative cells into resistant endospores
option_c: Asexual division of fertilized eggs inside maternal oviducts
option_d: Series of structural and physiological changes an organism undergoes from egg to adult
explanation: Metamorphosis is the developmental process marked by abrupt morphological, biochemical, and physiological transformations from larva to adult.
subject: Biology

question: Complete metamorphosis (holometabolous development) occurs in which of the following groups of insects?
option_a: Houseflies, butterflies, mosquitoes, and beetles
option_b: Cockroaches, grasshoppers, and termites
option_c: Dragonflies, damselflies, and praying mantises
option_d: Silverfish and springtails
explanation: Holometabolous insects undergo four distinct life stages: Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult (imago) (e.g. butterflies, mosquitoes, houseflies, honeybees).
subject: Biology

question: Incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetabolous development) involves which life cycle stages?
option_a: Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult
option_b: Egg → Nymph → Adult (imago)
option_c: Egg → Pupa → Nymph → Adult
option_d: Larva → Chrysalis → Imago only
explanation: Hemimetabolous insects (e.g. cockroaches, grasshoppers) exhibit three stages: Egg → Nymph (miniature wingless adult that moults) → Adult, lacking a pupal stage.
subject: Biology

question: The feeding, active, worm-like larval stage of a butterfly is known as a:
option_a: Maggot
option_b: Wriggler
option_c: Caterpillar
option_d: Grub
explanation: The larva of a butterfly/moth is a caterpillar; housefly larvae are maggots, mosquito larvae are wrigglers, and beetle larvae are grubs.
subject: Biology

question: The non-feeding, resting developmental stage in complete metamorphosis during which extensive tissue reorganization takes place is the:
option_a: Larva
option_b: Nymph
option_c: Imago
option_d: Pupa (chrysalis / cocoon)
explanation: The pupa is a quiescent stage where larval tissues histolyze and adult organ systems develop from imaginal discs before emergence.
subject: Biology

question: The larva of a mosquito that hangs beneath the water surface breathing through a respiratory siphon is commonly called a:
option_a: Wriggler
option_b: Tumbler
option_c: Caterpillar
option_d: Maggot
explanation: Mosquito larvae are wrigglers that breathe atmospheric air via a posterior siphon; the motile pupa is called a tumbler.
subject: Biology

question: Which insect hormone secreted by the prothoracic gland triggers moulting (ecdysis) and metamorphosis?
option_a: Juvenile hormone
option_b: Ecdysone (moulting hormone)
option_c: Bursicon
option_d: Insulin-like peptide
explanation: Ecdysone stimulates apolysis and synthesis of a new cuticular exoskeleton during ecdysis, working in concert with juvenile hormone.
subject: Biology

question: Juvenile hormone (JH) in insects is secreted by the corpora allata and functions to:
option_a: Trigger the immediate dissolution of the pupal cocoon shell
option_b: Stimulate adult female insects to search for nectar sources
option_c: Maintain larval characteristics and prevent premature metamorphosis into an adult
option_d: Halt all mitotic cell divisions in developing wing buds
explanation: High levels of juvenile hormone keep the insect in its larval stage during moults; when JH titers drop, ecdysone induces pupation and adult metamorphosis.
subject: Biology

question: During toad (amphibian) metamorphosis, which hormone secreted by the thyroid gland controls the transformation of an aquatic tadpole into a terrestrial adult?
option_a: Adrenaline
option_b: Growth hormone
option_c: Parathyroid hormone
option_d: Thyroxine
explanation: Thyroxine governs amphibian metamorphosis: stimulating tail resorption, limb bud outgrowth, gill degeneration, and lung development.
subject: Biology

question: Gregor Mendel is universally acclaimed as the father of modern genetics based on his hybridization experiments using the:
option_a: Garden pea plant (Pisum sativum)
option_b: Fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster)
option_c: Sweet corn plant (Zea mays)
option_d: Laboratory albino rat (Rattus norvegicus)
explanation: Gregor Mendel conducted quantitative inheritance experiments between 1856 and 1863 using the garden pea (Pisum sativum).
subject: Biology

question: Alternative forms of a gene located at the same relative locus on homologous chromosomes are called:
option_a: Chromatids
option_b: Alleles
option_c: Centromeres
option_d: Karyotypes
explanation: Alleles are alternative nucleotide sequences of a gene that govern the same trait and occupy corresponding loci on homologous chromosomes.
subject: Biology

question: The observable physical, physiological, or biochemical manifestation of an organism's genetic makeup is its:
option_a: Genotype
option_b: Genome
option_c: Phenotype
option_d: Haplotype
explanation: The phenotype represents the observable traits of an organism (e.g. tall, albino, round seeds), resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment.
subject: Biology

question: An organism possessing two identical alleles for a particular genetic trait (such as TT or tt) is described as:
option_a: Heterozygous
option_b: Hemizygous
option_c: Polygenic
option_d: Homozygous
explanation: Homozygosity denotes having identical alleles at a locus (homozygous dominant TT or homozygous recessive tt).
subject: Biology

question: Mendel's First Law of Inheritance—the Law of Segregation—states that:
option_a: Allele pairs separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele for each gene
option_b: Genes for different traits assort completely independently into daughter cells
option_c: Dominant alleles blend permanently with recessive alleles in the F1 generation
option_d: Acquired physical characteristics are passed directly to succeeding generations
explanation: The Law of Segregation states that during meiosis, the two alleles of each gene locus segregate from each other so each gamete carries only one allele.
subject: Biology

question: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt), what is the expected phenotypic ratio among the F2 offspring?
option_a: 1 Tall : 2 Medium : 1 Dwarf
option_b: 3 Tall : 1 Dwarf
option_c: 1 Tall : 1 Dwarf
option_d: 9 Tall : 3 Dwarf
explanation: The Punnett square of Tt × Tt yields 1 TT, 2 Tt, and 1 tt: a phenotypic ratio of 3 tall (TT, Tt) to 1 dwarf (tt).
subject: Biology

question: What is the expected genotypic ratio resulting from a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt × Tt)?
option_a: 3 TT : 1 tt
option_b: 1 Tt : 1 tt
option_d: 2 TT : 2 Tt
explanation: Crossing Tt with Tt produces a genotypic ratio of 1 homozygous dominant (TT) : 2 heterozygous (Tt) : 1 homozygous recessive (tt).
subject: Biology

question: A test cross is performed by crossing an organism showing a dominant phenotype with an organism that is:
option_a: Homozygous dominant for the same trait
option_b: Heterozygous for two unrelated traits
option_c: A sterile triploid hybrid
option_d: Homozygous recessive for the trait to determine the dominant individual's genotype
explanation: A test cross mates an individual of unknown dominant genotype (TT or Tt) with a homozygous recessive individual (tt); if recessive offspring appear, the parent is heterozygous.
subject: Biology

question: Mendel's Second Law—the Law of Independent Assortment—applies to dihybrid inheritance and predicts an F2 phenotypic ratio of:
explanation: In a dihybrid cross involving two unlinked heterozygous gene pairs (e.g. RrYy × RrYy), alleles assort independently to yield a classic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.
subject: Biology

question: Co-dominance is exemplified in human genetics by the inheritance of:
option_a: Huntington's chorea
option_b: ABO blood group AB (IAIB alleles expressing both A and B antigens)
option_c: Cystic fibrosis
option_d: Albinism in skin pigmentation
explanation: In co-dominance, both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote without blending; individuals with genotype IAIB express both A and B erythrocyte antigens.
subject: Biology

question: Incomplete dominance (partial dominance) is observed in Mirabilis jalapa (four o'clock flower) where crossing red-flowered and white-flowered plants yields F1 offspring with:
option_a: Pure red flowers only
option_b: Pure white flowers only
option_c: Pink flowers
option_d: Striped red-and-white petals
explanation: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is completely dominant; heterozygotes exhibit an intermediate blended phenotype (red CRCR × white CWCW → pink CRCW).
subject: Biology

question: How many pairs of autosomes are found in a normal somatic cell of a human being?
option_a: 23 pairs
option_b: 1 pair
option_c: 46 pairs
option_d: 22 pairs (44 autosomes)
explanation: Normal human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes: 22 homologous pairs of autosomes (44 chromosomes) and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
subject: Biology

question: Human biological sex is determined at fertilization by the male gamete because:
option_a: Spermatozoa carry either an X or a Y chromosome, whereas all ova carry an X chromosome
option_b: Ova carry both X and Y chromosomes simultaneously
option_c: The Y chromosome is donated exclusively by the maternal mitochondria
option_d: Female ova actively select which sperm cell penetrates the vitelline membrane
explanation: Human females are homogametic (XX, producing only X-bearing eggs); males are heterogametic (XY, producing 50% X-bearing and 50% Y-bearing sperm).
subject: Biology

question: Red-green colour blindness and hemophilia are classic examples of human genetic disorders that are:
option_a: Autosomal dominant traits inherited equally by both sexes
option_b: Sex-linked recessive traits carried on the non-homologous portion of the X chromosome
option_c: Y-linked holandric traits transmitted solely from mother to daughter
option_d: Mitochondrial disorders transmitted exclusively through paternal lineages
explanation: Sex-linked recessive traits reside on the X chromosome; because males have only one X chromosome (hemizygous), they manifest the condition much more frequently than females.
subject: Biology

question: If a man with normal vision marries a woman who is a carrier for red-green colour blindness (XCXc), what is the probability that their son will be colour blind?
explanation: Sons receive their single X chromosome from their mother. A carrier mother has a 50% chance of passing the mutant Xc allele to a son, making him colour blind (XcY).
subject: Biology

question: Continuous variation in a population is characterized by:
option_a: Clear-cut distinct phenotypic categories with no overlapping intermediates
option_b: Traits determined entirely by a single pair of non-interacting alleles
option_c: Phenotypes that remain completely unaffected by environmental factors
option_d: A complete gradient of intermediate phenotypes between two extremes without distinct categories (e.g. human height and skin colour)
explanation: Continuous variation (e.g. height, weight, intelligence) is polygenic and quantitative, displaying a bell-shaped normal distribution curve across a population.
subject: Biology

question: Which of the following human traits is an example of discontinuous variation?
option_a: ABO blood groups and tongue-rolling ability
option_b: Body height and mass
option_c: Skin pigmentation and foot length
option_d: Blood pressure and resting pulse rate
explanation: Discontinuous variation features discrete, clear-cut categories governed by one or two genes with minimal environmental influence (e.g. blood groups, tongue rolling).
subject: Biology

question: A sudden, permanent, and heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of an organism's DNA is termed a:
option_a: Recombination
option_b: Mutation
option_c: Adaptation
option_d: Translocation
explanation: A mutation is a spontaneous or induced permanent alteration in the genomic sequence, creating novel alleles and generating genetic diversity.
subject: Biology

question: Sickle cell anemia in humans is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene where:
option_a: Cytosine is deleted, producing a premature stop codon
option_b: An entire extra chromosome 21 is gained during non-disjunction
option_c: Adenine is substituted by thymine, replacing glutamic acid with valine at position 6
option_d: Histone proteins are completely deleted from chromatin threads
explanation: Sickle cell anemia results from a point mutation (GAG → GTG) in the HBB gene, substituting hydrophobic valine for hydrophilic glutamic acid at codon 6 of beta-globin.
subject: Biology

question: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) in humans is a chromosomal aberration caused by:
option_a: Point mutation in the rhodopsin gene on chromosome 3
option_b: Duplication of the androgen receptor gene on the Y chromosome
option_c: Loss of the short arm of chromosome 5
option_d: Non-disjunction of chromosome pair 21 during meiotic division
explanation: Down syndrome results from non-disjunction during maternal oogenesis, leading to an extra copy of chromosome 21 (total 47 chromosomes: 47, XX,+21 or 47, XY,+21).
subject: Biology

question: Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal disorder in males characterized by the karyotype:
option_a: 47, XXY
option_c: 47, XYY
option_d: 46, XX
explanation: Klinefelter syndrome males possess an extra X chromosome (47, XXY), exhibiting tall stature, reduced testosterone, gynecomastia, and infertility.
subject: Biology

question: Turner syndrome is a female genetic disorder characterized by which karyotype?
option_a: 47, XXX
option_b: 45, X0 (monosomy X)
option_c: 47, XXY
option_d: 46, XY
explanation: Turner syndrome females have a missing sex chromosome (45, X0), presenting with short stature, webbed neck, underdeveloped ovaries, and amenorrhea.
subject: Biology

question: A mutagen is an environmental agent that increases the frequency of mutations; examples include:
option_a: Distilled water and sodium chloride solution
option_b: Glucose syrups and liquid vegetable oil
option_c: X-rays, ultraviolet radiation, and mustard gas
option_d: Atmospheric nitrogen and carbon dioxide gases
explanation: Mutagens include ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), UV light, and chemical mutagens (benzene, nitrosamines, alkylating agents) that alter DNA.
subject: Biology

question: Chromosomal inversion occurs when a chromosomal segment:
option_a: Is completely lost during unequal meiotic crossing over
option_b: Transfers onto a non-homologous chromosome entirely
option_c: Replicates three times to produce tandem repeating arrays
option_d: Breaks off, rotates 180 degrees, and reattaches in reverse orientation
explanation: An inversion is a chromosomal rearrangement in which a segment breaks off, flips end-to-end (180°), and rejoins the same chromosome.
subject: Biology

question: Albinism in humans is inherited as an:
option_a: Autosomal recessive trait causing deficiency of the pigment melanin
option_b: Autosomal dominant trait causing hyper-pigmentation
option_c: X-linked recessive disorder occurring exclusively in males
option_d: Infectious viral disease of the skin epidermis
explanation: Albinism is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a lack of the enzyme tyrosinase, preventing melanin synthesis in skin, hair, and eyes.
subject: Biology

question: Heterozygote advantage (hybrid vigor) is observed in regions where malaria is endemic because individuals with genotype HbAS (sickle cell trait):
option_a: Are completely immune to all bacterial and fungal infections
option_b: Possess higher resistance to severe falciparum malaria than normal homozygotes (HbAA)
option_c: Produce twice the normal concentration of adult hemoglobin
option_d: Cannot be bitten by female Anopheles mosquitoes
explanation: Heterozygous HbAS individuals enjoy a survival advantage (balanced polymorphism) against fatal malaria compared to HbAA, while avoiding full sickle cell disease (HbSS).
subject: Biology

question: Polyploidy, which is common and beneficial in cultivated crop plants (such as wheat and bananas), results in:
option_a: Complete failure of plants to photosynthesize in daylight
option_b: Severe dwarfing and immediate lethality in all plant tissues
option_c: Increased cell size, vigorous vegetative growth, and larger fruits or seeds
option_d: Loss of all resistance against common agricultural fungal pests
explanation: Polyploidy often produces the 'gigas' effect: larger cells, sturdier stems, enhanced drought tolerance, and dramatically larger flowers, fruits, and grains.
subject: Biology

question: The theory of evolution by natural selection was independently formulated and published by Charles Darwin and:
option_a: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
option_b: Thomas Malthus
option_c: Louis Pasteur
option_d: Alfred Russel Wallace
explanation: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently formulated the theory of evolution by natural selection, presenting joint papers in London in 1858.
subject: Biology

question: The French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that evolution occurs through the:
option_a: Inheritance of acquired characteristics and the principle of use and disuse
option_b: Survival of the fittest through differential reproductive success
option_c: Spontaneous occurrence of polyploid chromosomal mutations
option_d: Random genetic drift in small, isolated island populations
explanation: Lamarckism proposed that organs developed through use or degenerated through disuse, and these acquired somatic changes were passed to offspring (now disproven).
subject: Biology

question: Darwin's theory of natural selection is founded on which core observations?
option_a: Sudden meiotic mutations that transform one species into another overnight
option_b: Overproduction of offspring, struggle for existence, variation among individuals, and survival of the fittest
option_c: The complete absence of competition for food and space in nature
option_d: Direct inheritance of surgically acquired phenotypic mutilations
explanation: Darwin observed that organisms produce more offspring than can survive, leading to a struggle for resources where individuals with advantageous variations survive and reproduce.
subject: Biology

question: Homologous structures in comparative anatomy (such as the pentadactyl limbs of humans, bats, whales, and horses) provide evidence of:
option_a: Convergent evolution from completely unrelated phyla
option_b: Independent creation with identical mechanical functions
option_c: Divergent evolution from a common ancestral body plan
option_d: Direct Lamarckian adaptation to aquatic swimming environments
explanation: Homologous organs share a common underlying anatomical architecture inherited from a common ancestor, adapted for different functions (divergent evolution).
subject: Biology

question: Analogous structures (such as the wings of a butterfly and the wings of a bird) demonstrate:
option_a: Direct descent from a common winged flying ancestor
option_b: Identical embryonic origins and skeletal arrangements
option_c: Vestigial structures that have lost their biological utility
option_d: Convergent evolution where unrelated organisms evolve similar adaptations for a common function
explanation: Analogous organs perform similar functions (flight) and look superficially alike but have distinct evolutionary and embryonic origins (convergent evolution).
subject: Biology

question: Vestigial organs in humans (such as the vermiform appendix, coccyx, and wisdom teeth) provide evidence for evolution because they:
option_a: Represent reduced, non-functional remnants of organs that were fully functional in ancestral species
option_b: Are actively evolving new vital physiological functions for modern life
option_c: Are present only in individuals suffering from rare genetic defects
option_d: Are formed exclusively in response to bacterial parasitic infections
explanation: Vestigial structures are anatomical remnants that served important functions in evolutionary ancestors but are now reduced and largely functionless.
subject: Biology

question: The fossil record provides direct, tangible evidence of organic evolution because it reveals:
option_a: That all modern living species appeared simultaneously in the earliest rocks
option_b: The chronological progression and morphological changes of organisms over geological time
option_c: That primitive ancestral organisms were physically larger than modern species
option_d: The precise mathematical equations governing Mendelian gene frequencies
explanation: Fossils preserved in sedimentary rock strata chronicle the history of life, showing transitional forms and progressive morphological changes over millions of years.
subject: Biology

question: Archaeopteryx is celebrated as a classic transitional fossil ('missing link') showing evolutionary features of both:
option_a: Fish and amphibians
option_b: Amphibians and reptiles
option_c: Reptiles and birds
option_d: Reptiles and mammals
explanation: Archaeopteryx possessed reptilian features (teeth, clawed fingers, long bony tail) and avian features (flight feathers, wishbone, wings), linking reptiles to birds.
subject: Biology

question: Industrial melanism in the peppered moth (Biston betularia) in England is a classic demonstration of:
option_a: Artificial selection by commercial silk manufacturers
option_b: Lamarckian inheritance of soot pigments across generations
option_c: Non-disjunction of sex chromosomes in lepidopterans
option_d: Natural selection in response to environmental pollution changes
explanation: During the Industrial Revolution, soot darkened tree trunks; melanic (black) moths had better camouflage from predatory birds, increasing dramatically in frequency.
subject: Biology

question: Comparative embryology provides evidence for evolution because the early embryonic stages of all vertebrates:
option_a: Exhibit striking similarities, including pharyngeal gill pouches and post-anal tails
option_b: Develop identical adult nervous and circulatory structures
option_c: Can interbreed successfully to produce viable hybrid offspring
option_d: Are completely indistinguishable from adult invertebrate worms
explanation: Vertebrate embryos (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, humans) all possess pharyngeal arches, post-anal tails, and similar somites, reflecting shared ancestry.
subject: Biology

question: Molecular biological evidence supporting universal common ancestry of all cellular life includes the:
option_a: Presence of identical bony endoskeletons in all living phyla
option_b: Universality of the genetic code and ATP as the universal energy currency
option_c: Equal ratio of red and white blood cells across all animal classes
option_d: Identical environmental temperature requirements across all species
explanation: All cellular life shares universal biochemical foundations: double-stranded DNA, universal 64-codon genetic code, 20 amino acids, and ATP as the primary energy currency.
subject: Biology

question: An ecosystem is best defined as a:
option_a: Collection of similar organisms of the same species inhabiting an area
option_b: Single food chain operating within a closed laboratory aquarium
option_c: Dynamic community of living organisms interacting with their non-living physical environment
option_d: Geographical zone characterized exclusively by abiotic climatic factors
explanation: An ecosystem comprises the biotic community (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components (soil, water, climate) functioning as a self-sustaining unit.
subject: Biology

question: In any ecological food chain, green plants occupy which trophic level?
option_a: Second trophic level (primary consumers)
option_b: Third trophic level (secondary consumers)
option_c: Top trophic level (apex decomposers)
option_d: First trophic level (primary producers)
